items.summary:
The last time we got a decent look at Total War: Warhammer 40,000 was the Gamescom build, which Fraser Brown called the highlight of his year . Since then Creative Assembly has continued iterating and a more recent build was subject to a friends-and-family playtest, then shown off in an "alpha strike" livestream that lasted a solid hour and 20 minutes.

Beginning 23 turns into an Ultramarines campaign, we got to see the battle for the Praevoss system, which has three conquerable planets in it—as well as a gas giant and a dead world that can't be fought over. 

Each system in Total War: Warhammer 40,000 gets a separate narrative, a mini-campaign that plays out before you move on to the next system, taking some but not all of what you've built with you. That seems like an interesting way of dealing with the grand strategy problem of campaigns getting boring when you've painted half the map, but still have 100 turns before the end. Having a soft reset and facing different foes in a different theatre would keep a campaign feeling fresh.

In the Praevoss system the Ultramarines' objective is to liberate Imperial planets from an ork scourge. When the marines take a region, one of the options they have is to "scour the battlefield" in return for a big payout in Requisition, at the cost of raised Suspicion. Calling down a fleet bombardment to soften up orks ahead of the battle also raises Suspicion because there are still civilians in the area. Oops.

items.title: GTA 6 Doesn't Let Players Pick Up Prostitutes, but Rockstar Has a Logical Reason for It
items.summary:
Rockstar Games has revealed why they chose to forego the ability to pick up prostitutes in GTA 6 .

That's right — GTA 6 doesn't let you pick up ladies of the night when you're feeling lonely anymore. No, the reason isn't because the game has "gone woke" or anything like that; instead, it's for narrative purposes. As you may already know, Rockstar has put the focus of GTA 6 on a couple. The entire story largely hinges on the romantic pair at the very least having an interest of pursuing a relationship with each other, if not being madly in love, should the player take them down that road. As a result, it wouldn't make much sense to have them out there cheating on each other in dark alleys.

Although Michael was a married man in GTA 5, he was not happily married, and spent most of the story dealing with the fact that his own wife cheated on him. Rockstar issued a statement to Shacknews about its decision to remove some features that were in previous GTA games, such as the ability to pick up prostitutes.

“GTA 6 is a game about a couple in a bind, lovers on the run," reads Rockstar's statement. "While we have taken a lot forward from previous GTA titles, everything we have implemented in 6 has been done to support the spirit of the story we wanted to tell, and the gameplay systems we wanted to expand upon - things like wanted system, the radio, robberies and car theft. Many aspects of previous titles are not present in GTA 6, but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasize as you play through Jason…

What makes the better Universes Beyond crossovers work is how they bring out the themes of their source material, turning motifs into mechanics that make a set feel like a genuine expression of the thing being adapted rather than just another property being fed into the content machine. Having played some games with the cards, yeah, I think Star Trek works.

I built a blue-green deck around Strange New Worlds , a mechanic that rewards you for having different lands rather than just stacking Islands and Forests. When I played Deep Space Scan I drew a card for each differently named land I had, and those lands also lowered the cost of powering up my Astute Terraformer. 

Meanwhile, the Federation mechanic gives bonuses for having different creature types on the table like Vulcan and Klingon and Romulan (though not Borg). Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, lead writer of the hit 2025 RPG Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , has revealed that she is no longer with developer Sandfall Interactive. In an interview with Gamesbeat , Svedberg-Yen said she wants to return to her own creative efforts, including stories for film and television, and also aims to set up a new fund specifically to support the advancement of narrative design in games.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was universally acclaimed and won an astounding list of awards, including just about every narrative-focused prize you can name: Best Storytelling at the Golden Joysticks, Best Narrative at The Game Awards, Outstanding Achievement in Story at DICE, Best Narrative at the GDC Awards, Best Narrative at the BAFTAs, and Hugo and Nebula awards. Game industry legend Warren Spector retired in August , and somewhat ironically he's been more outspoken than ever about the state of the games industry. After blowing up over the closure of BioWare in October, he took a few weeks to think about it and got even more pissed off —and now he's shared some thoughts on the biggest videogame release of all time, Grand Theft Auto 6 .

Unlike the BioWare mess, Spector's not angry about GTA 6, but he's clearly ambivalent: His latest missive on LinkedIn opens with a congratulations to the dev team and says, "It looks like it will be a high point of sorts for our medium and our business," which right out of the gate suggests that he's not entirely upbeat about it.

Spector wasted no time getting to the point. "Its billion-dollar development cost and an undoubtedly crazy marketing budget don't represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate," he wrote. The safe codes you need in the main story or specific missions are given to you, but in order to get a safe code during a robbery (and you'll need to because they're randomised), you have two main options:

Find the code written down on the premises Interrogate an employee to get it First off, you can sometimes find the code written on something inside the store or bank, like a note on a board in the back office perhaps, or maybe a guard you've incapacitated is carrying it—press L3 and R3 to activate Focus Mode and help you find it.

You can also get the code by interrogating employees. Aim your weapon at them and use the "Threaten" or "Safe Code?" prompt shown on the screen to force them to give you the information. In certain robberies, this will also force cashiers to empty the register, as in previous GTA games.

Once you have the safe code, it will appear in the lower right corner of the screen when you're interacting with the safe. You'll have to enter the four-digit code to unlock it.

Time is of the essence, so the faster you can get the code, the quicker you can open the safe and load the cash into your bag. items.title: World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth , the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! items.title: I have double-checked and yes, original 'GTA killer' Driv3r really was that rubbish
items.summary:
At this point the tragedy of Driv3r , or Driver 3, or my personal favourite Drive-thrur, is well thumbed. A familiar litany of unrealised ambition, heinous bugs, dull open-world design, and an expensive yet audibly bored voice cast, the accidental comedic highlight of which is Michelle Rodriguez flatly reeling off car theft orders from what sounds like the inside of a Michelle Rodriguez-sized tupperware container.

A more widely forgotten detail is that, for a while, there was a non-zero chance - a belief, even - that Drive Three Er was going to be the opposite. The 2003-2004 hype cycle had sowed the notion that this would in fact be the open-world crime thriller to knock Grand Theft Auto off its perch, and even 22 years before GTA 6 's idolising reviews , that was no small promise; Rockstar were still enjoying the balmy success of Vice City, and we could see San Andreas cresting the hill on a stolen, shining BMX. "Ah, but did they have Michael Madsen doing doughnuts in car parks?," publishers Atari asked the world, either unaware or in denial of the spluttering, clapped-out rattletrap they were about to wheel into the showroom.

You likely know the rest, though one of the dangers of familiarity is the subsequent breeding of complacency, which in this case can manifest as a thawing acceptance. I succumbed to this myself, having recently installed a legally unlinkable copy of Drivethreeuh, mind opened to the possibility that maybe it wasn't that bad. Six hours later, I am here to tell you: it was.

Frankly, it's bizarre to think of Rockstar working on games that aren't GTA 6 , which rolls onto console hard drives this week. A decade in the making, with a development team of thousands scattered across an international network of studios, GTA 6 aims to be the Maximum Game. It's both a dense, lively open world and a monument to the exhausting impersonality of "triple-A" game productions. It contains multitudes: birdlife! Realistic cloud formation! Fuel mechanics! Romance! Soda visibly sloshing around in bottles! It's an imperial production shadowed by labour disputes , that appears to have given Rockstar's various teams little time or space to think about anything else.

It wasn't ever thus. Once upon a time, Rockstar weren't just known for GTA and to a considerably lesser extent, Red Dead Redemption . Once upon a time, they had a reputation for slightly dodgy experiments. I recently interviewed former Rockstar North tech director Obbe Vermeij about a few of them, including Agent, the unofficial James Bond game Rockstar toyed with before putting all chips on Grand Theft Auto 5 .

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics , together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus . Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.
